claim: Dopamine (DA) neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) play a pivotal role in signaling reward-related stimuli.
source: Dopamine (DA) neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) play a pivotal role in signaling reward-related stimuli (Wise, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wise, 2004

claim: Alterations in the function of VTA DA neurons have been linked to drug abuse.
source: Alterations in the function of VTA DA neurons have been linked to drug abuse (Kauer and Malenka, 2007; Niehaus et al., 2009), as well as neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders including autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) (Bariselli et al., 2016), schizophrenia, and depression (Grace, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kauer and Malenka, 2007; Niehaus et al., 2009

claim: Alterations in the function of VTA DA neurons have been linked to autism spectrum disorders (ASDs).
source: Alterations in the function of VTA DA neurons have been linked to drug abuse (Kauer and Malenka, 2007; Niehaus et al., 2009), as well as neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders including autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) (Bariselli et al., 2016), schizophrenia, and depression (Grace, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bariselli et al., 2016

claim: Alterations in the function of VTA DA neurons have been linked to schizophrenia and depression.
source: Alterations in the function of VTA DA neurons have been linked to drug abuse (Kauer and Malenka, 2007; Niehaus et al., 2009), as well as neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders including autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) (Bariselli et al., 2016), schizophrenia, and depression (Grace, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grace, 2016

claim: DA neurons exhibit two activity patterns in vivo – low frequency tonic firing (1–5 Hz) and burst, or phasic, firing patterns.
source: DA neurons exhibit two activity patterns in vivo – low frequency tonic firing (1–5 Hz) and burst, or phasic, firing patterns (Floresco et al., 2003; Grace and Bunney, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Floresco et al., 2003; Grace and Bunney, 1984

claim: Phasic activity of DA neurons is observed when an animal is in an environment with strong reward salience.
source: Phasic activity of DA neurons is observed when an animal is in an environment with strong reward salience (Schultz, 1998; Schultz et al., 2015), resulting in large transient increases in DA concentration in the ventral striatum.
evidence: Supported by citations to Schultz, 1998; Schultz et al., 2015

claim: Phasic activity of DA neurons results in large transient increases in DA concentration in the ventral striatum.
source: Phasic activity of DA neurons is observed when an animal is in an environment with strong reward salience (Schultz, 1998; Schultz et al., 2015), resulting in large transient increases in DA concentration in the ventral striatum.
evidence: Supported by citations to Schultz, 1998; Schultz et al., 2015

claim: DA increases in the ventral striatum have been directly assayed using fast-scan cyclic voltammetry.
source: These DA increases have been directly assayed using fast-scan cyclic voltammetry (Tsai et al., 2009) and are well-matched by recent optical imaging studies that demonstrate unpredicted reward-associated calcium transients in the axons of VTA DA neurons expressing genetically encoded calcium sensors (Howe and Dombeck, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsai et al., 2009

claim: Recent optical imaging studies demonstrate unpredicted reward-associated calcium transients in the axons of VTA DA neurons expressing genetically encoded calcium sensors.
source: These DA increases have been directly assayed using fast-scan cyclic voltammetry (Tsai et al., 2009) and are well-matched by recent optical imaging studies that demonstrate unpredicted reward-associated calcium transients in the axons of VTA DA neurons expressing genetically encoded calcium sensors (Howe and Dombeck, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howe and Dombeck, 2016

claim: Glutamatergic afferents to DA neurons are thought to control transitions between tonic and phasic activity.
source: Glutamatergic afferents to DA neurons are thought to control transitions between tonic and phasic activity (Canavier and Landry, 2006; Floresco et al., 2003; Overton and Clark, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Canavier and Landry, 2006; Floresco et al., 2003; Overton and Clark, 1997

claim: Glutamatergic inputs to the VTA arise from multiple brain regions, including the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), lateral habenular nucleus (LHb) and pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPN).
source: For the VTA, these inputs arise from multiple brain regions, including the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), lateral habenular nucleus (LHb) and pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPN) (Geisler et al., 2007; Good and Lupica, 2009; Morales and Margolis, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geisler et al., 2007; Good and Lupica, 2009; Morales and Margolis, 2017

claim: VTA DA neurons express dopamine Drd2 receptor.
source: VTA DA neurons express numerous GPCRs, including dopamine Drd2 receptor (Vallone et al., 2000), as well as receptors for serotonin (Doherty and Pickel, 2000), corticotropin-releasing factor (Ungless et al., 2003), orexin (Korotkova et al., 2003), vasopressin, and oxytocin (Skuse and Gallagher, 2009; Xiao et al., 2017), among others.
evidence: Supported by citation to Vallone et al., 2000

claim: VTA DA neurons express receptors for serotonin.
source: VTA DA neurons express numerous GPCRs, including dopamine Drd2 receptor (Vallone et al., 2000), as well as receptors for serotonin (Doherty and Pickel, 2000), corticotropin-releasing factor (Ungless et al., 2003), orexin (Korotkova et al., 2003), vasopressin, and oxytocin (Skuse and Gallagher, 2009; Xiao et al., 2017), among others.
evidence: Supported by citation to Doherty and Pickel, 2000

claim: VTA DA neurons express receptors for corticotropin-releasing factor.
source: VTA DA neurons express numerous GPCRs, including dopamine Drd2 receptor (Vallone et al., 2000), as well as receptors for serotonin (Doherty and Pickel, 2000), corticotropin-releasing factor (Ungless et al., 2003), orexin (Korotkova et al., 2003), vasopressin, and oxytocin (Skuse and Gallagher, 2009; Xiao et al., 2017), among others.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ungless et al., 2003

claim: VTA DA neurons express receptors for orexin.
source: VTA DA neurons express numerous GPCRs, including dopamine Drd2 receptor (Vallone et al., 2000), as well as receptors for serotonin (Doherty and Pickel, 2000), corticotropin-releasing factor (Ungless et al., 2003), orexin (Korotkova et al., 2003), vasopressin, and oxytocin (Skuse and Gallagher, 2009; Xiao et al., 2017), among others.
evidence: Supported by citation to Korotkova et al., 2003

claim: VTA DA neurons express receptors for vasopressin and oxytocin.
source: VTA DA neurons express numerous GPCRs, including dopamine Drd2 receptor (Vallone et al., 2000), as well as receptors for serotonin (Doherty and Pickel, 2000), corticotropin-releasing factor (Ungless et al., 2003), orexin (Korotkova et al., 2003), vasopressin, and oxytocin (Skuse and Gallagher, 2009; Xiao et al., 2017), among others.
evidence: Supported by citations to Skuse and Gallagher, 2009; Xiao et al., 2017

claim: Several GPCR families are known to modulate neuronal activity and synaptic transmission in VTA DA neurons.
source: Several GPCR families are known to modulate neuronal activity and synaptic transmission in VTA DA neurons (Bonci and Malenka, 1999; Borgland et al., 2006; Ungless et al., 2003), but our understanding of how neurohypophyseal peptides control synaptic transmission in the midbrain dopamine system is limited.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonci and Malenka, 1999; Borgland et al., 2006; Ungless et al., 2003

claim: Oxytocin functions centrally as a neuromodulator and has been linked to the processing of socially rewarding stimuli via actions in the striatum and in the neocortex.
source: Oxytocin is one of the two major neurohypophyseal peptides that function centrally as a neuromodulator and has been linked to the processing of socially rewarding stimuli via actions in the striatum and in the neocortex (Choe et al., 2015; Dölen et al., 2013; Marlin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Choe et al., 2015; Dölen et al., 2013; Marlin et al., 2015

claim: In the nucleus accumbens, oxytocin weakens glutamatergic synaptic transmission through presynaptic mechanisms involving serotonergic inputs from the dorsal raphe nucleus.
source: In the nucleus accumbens, oxytocin weakens glutamatergic synaptic transmission through presynaptic mechanisms involving serotonergic inputs from the dorsal raphe nucleus (Dölen et al., 2013), and in the mPFC, oxytocin application dampens glutamatergic synaptic transmission through presynaptic endocannabinoid signaling (Ninan, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dölen et al., 2013

claim: In the mPFC, oxytocin application dampens glutamatergic synaptic transmission through presynaptic endocannabinoid signaling.
source: In the nucleus accumbens, oxytocin weakens glutamatergic synaptic transmission through presynaptic mechanisms involving serotonergic inputs from the dorsal raphe nucleus (Dölen et al., 2013), and in the mPFC, oxytocin application dampens glutamatergic synaptic transmission through presynaptic endocannabinoid signaling (Ninan, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ninan, 2011

claim: In the auditory and piriform cortex, oxytocin application or evoked release dampen inhibitory transmission without altering excitatory input processing.
source: Yet, in the auditory and piriform cortex, oxytocin application or evoked release dampen inhibitory transmission without altering excitatory input processing (Mitre et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mitre et al., 2016

claim: Oxytocin neurons residing in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) directly project to the VTA and activate oxytocin receptors (OxtRs) to regulate the tonic activity of DA neurons and social behavior.
source: Oxytocin neurons residing in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) directly project to the VTA and activate oxytocin receptors (OxtRs) to regulate the tonic activity of DA neurons and social behavior (Beier et al., 2015; Hung et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beier et al., 2015; Hung et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2017

claim: Oxytocin infusions into the VTA potentiate social reward.
source: Consistent with oxytocin-driven enhancement in the activity of VTA DA neurons, oxytocin infusions into the VTA potentiate social reward (Song et al., 2016) and modulate reward-based behavior (Mullis et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2016

claim: Oxytocin infusions into the VTA modulate reward-based behavior.
source: Consistent with oxytocin-driven enhancement in the activity of VTA DA neurons, oxytocin infusions into the VTA potentiate social reward (Song et al., 2016) and modulate reward-based behavior (Mullis et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mullis et al., 2013

claim: OxtR agonist was found to regulate synaptic inputs to a specific subpopulation of VTA DA neurons that project to medial nucleus accumbens, altering the balance of excitation and inhibition.
source: Recently, OxtR agonist was found to regulate synaptic inputs to a specific subpopulation of VTA DA neurons that project to medial nucleus accumbens, altering the balance of excitation and inhibition through cellular mechanisms that remain incompletely understood (Hung et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hung et al., 2017

claim: Bath application of 1 μM oxytocin significantly reduced the amplitude of evoked EPSCs to 77.43 ± 1.55% of baseline (p<0.001, n = 15 neurons from 10 mice).
source: Bath application of 1 μM oxytocin significantly reduced the amplitude of evoked EPSCs (77.43 ± 1.55% of baseline, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 15 neurons from 10 mice) (Figure 1A,B and F), without changing the input resistance of VTA DA neurons or decay time constant of EPSCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: Oxytocin application did not change the input resistance of VTA DA neurons or decay time constant of EPSCs.
source: Bath application of 1 μM oxytocin significantly reduced the amplitude of evoked EPSCs (77.43 ± 1.55% of baseline, p<0.001, paired t-test, n = 15 neurons from 10 mice) (Figure 1A,B and F), without changing the input resistance of VTA DA neurons or decay time constant of EPSCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F

claim: Oxytocin-induced EPSC depression in VTA DA neurons was similar in males and females.
source: This oxytocin-induced EPSC depression in VTA DA neurons was similar in males and females (♂, 79.12 ± 5.58% of baseline, n = 5 neurons; ♀, 77.36 ± 3.39% of baseline, n = 10 neurons. p=0.440, Mann-Whitney test), consistent with a prior report on sex invariance of oxytocinergic regulation of midbrain DA systems in structure and function (Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and citation to Xiao et al., 2017

claim: Oxytocin application in concentrations at or above 100 nM is sufficient to decrease EPSC amplitude in a dose-dependent manner.
source: To build a dose-response curve we also evaluated the effect of oxytocin on excitatory synaptic transmission at concentrations below 1 µM (0 nM, 10 nM, 100 nM, and 500 nM), and observed that oxytocin application in concentrations at or above 100 nM is sufficient to decrease EPSC amplitude in a dose-dependent manner (0 nM, 103.50 ± 3.05% of baseline; 10 nM, 94.74 ± 1.38% of baseline; 100 nM, 87.73 ± 0.88% of baseline; 500 nM, 83.31 ± 3.18% of baseline, p<0.01, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's Multiple Comparison post hoc test, n = 5–8 neurons from 2 to 5 mice/group) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1F

claim: In the presence of OxtR antagonist (10 μM L368,899), bath application of 1 μM oxytocin did not have a significant effect on the amplitude of evoked EPSCs (98.89 ± 3.39% of baseline, p=0.844, n = 8 neurons from six mice).
source: In the presence of OxtR antagonist (10 μM L368,899) we observed that bath application of 1 μM oxytocin did not have a significant effect on the amplitude of evoked EPSCs (98.89 ± 3.39% of baseline, p=0.844, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 8 neurons from six mice) (Figure 1C and G, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1C and G

claim: OxtR antagonist application alone had no effect on the amplitude of evoked EPSCs.
source: OxtR antagonist application alone had no effect on the amplitude of evoked EPSCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), which suggests that no oxytocin tone is present in the acute brain slice of the VTA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: No oxytocin tone is present in the acute brain slice of the VTA.
source: OxtR antagonist application alone had no effect on the amplitude of evoked EPSCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), which suggests that no oxytocin tone is present in the acute brain slice of the VTA.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of OxtR antagonist alone

claim: OxtRs primarily couple to Gαq protein effectors, which activate the phospholipase C (PLC) pathway to mobilize intracellular Ca2+ store release.
source: OxtRs primarily couple to Gαq protein effectors, which activate the phospholipase C (PLC) pathway to mobilize intracellular Ca2+ store release (Gimpl and Fahrenholz, 2001; Stoop, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gimpl and Fahrenholz, 2001; Stoop, 2012

claim: In the presence of 10 μM U73122 (PLC inhibitor), oxytocin failed to decrease evoked EPSC amplitude (98.92 ± 5.33% of baseline, p=0.949, n = 5 neurons from four mice).
source: In the presence of 10 μM U73122, oxytocin failed to decrease evoked EPSC amplitude (98.92 ± 5.33% of baseline, p=0.949, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 5 neurons from four mice) (Figure 1D and G, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D and G

claim: Oxytocin binds to Gαq protein-coupled OxtR to regulate synaptic transmission in VTA DA neurons through the canonical PLC pathway.
source: Thus, oxytocin binds to Gαq protein-coupled OxtR to regulate synaptic transmission in VTA DA neurons through the canonical PLC pathway.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results with OxtR antagonist and PLC inhibitor

claim: Vasopressin 1a receptor (V1aR) transcripts are present in the rodent VTA, including in DA neurons.
source: Indeed, vasopressin 1a receptor (V1aR) transcripts are present in the rodent VTA, including in DA neurons (Dubois-Dauphin et al., 1996; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dubois-Dauphin et al., 1996; Xiao et al., 2017

claim: In the presence of V1aR antagonist (10 μM SR49059), oxytocin application decreased the amplitude of the evoked EPSCs to 80.94 ± 2.33% of baseline (p<0.001, n = 9 neurons from six mice).
source: Under these conditions, oxytocin application decreased the amplitude of the evoked EPSCs to the same degree as in the baseline condition (80.94 ± 2.33% of baseline, p<0.001, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 9 neurons from six mice) (Figure 1E and G, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E and G

claim: PVN oxytocin neuron projections that co-release glutamate have been reported in the parabrachial nucleus.
source: PVN oxytocin neuron projections that co-release glutamate have been reported in the parabrachial nucleus (Ryan et al., 2017) and in brainstem vagal neurons (Piñol et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2017

claim: PVN oxytocin neuron projections that co-release glutamate have been reported in brainstem vagal neurons.
source: PVN oxytocin neuron projections that co-release glutamate have been reported in the parabrachial nucleus (Ryan et al., 2017) and in brainstem vagal neurons (Piñol et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Piñol et al., 2014

claim: No fast responses in VTA DA cells were observed in response to single 10 ms-long light pulses to optically stimulate PVN oxytocin fibers (light-evoked response change −0.556 ± 0.285 pA, p=0.303, n = 16 neurons from five mice).
source: In contrast to parabrachial and vagal neurons, no fast responses in VTA DA cells were observed (light-evoked response change −0.556 ± 0.285 pA, p=0.303, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test; n = 16 neurons from five mice).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: Optical stimulation of oxytocin fibers depolarized VTA DA neurons in voltage-clamp recordings, evidenced by a small but consistent change in holding current (2.955 ± 0.871 pA, p<0.01, n = 15 neurons from eight mice).
source: Optical stimulation of oxytocin fibers depolarized VTA DA neurons in voltage-clamp recordings, evidenced by a small but consistent change in holding current (2.955 ± 0.871 pA, p<0.01, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 15 neurons from eight mice), consistent with prior observations of tonic activity changes in VTA DA neurons in response to oxytocin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: The amplitude of evoked EPSC in VTA DA neurons was decreased 30 s after optical stimulation of oxytocin fibers (61.71 ± 4.39% of baseline, p<0.01, n = 9 neurons from six mice).
source: As for bath application experiments, we observed that the amplitude of evoked EPSC in VTA DA neurons was decreased, evident 30 s after optical stimulation (61.71 ± 4.39% of baseline, p<0.01, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 9 neurons from six mice) (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1I

claim: The effect of optical stimulation of oxytocin fibers on EPSC amplitude was abolished in the presence of OxtR antagonist (L368,899) (114.30 ± 8.04% of baseline, p=0.156, n = 6 neurons from four mice).
source: This repeatable effect was abolished in the presence of OxtR antagonist (L368,899) (114.30 ± 8.04% of baseline, p=0.156, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 6 neurons from four mice) (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1I

claim: 30 s long light activation of oxytocinergic fibers in VTA is sufficient to lead to a relatively long-lasting decrease in the amplitude of EPSCs (5–15 min after light stimulation: 69.22 ± 6.72% of baseline; 15–25 min after light stimulation: 57.77 ± 7.01% of baseline, p<0.01, n = 6 neurons from four mice).
source: We also observed that 30 s long light activation of oxytocinergic fibers in VTA is sufficient to lead to a relatively long-lasting decrease in the amplitude of EPSCs (5–15 min after light stimulation: 69.22 ± 6.72% of baseline; 15–25 min after light stimulation: 57.77 ± 7.01% of baseline, p<0.01, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's Multiple Comparison post hoc test, n = 6 neurons from four mice) (Figure 1J–K, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1J–K

claim: Oxytocin application significantly increased PPR at a 50 ms ISI (Baseline, 1.120 ± 0.057; Oxt, 1.721 ± 0.116; p<0.01, n = 8 neurons from six mice).
source: Oxytocin application significantly increased PPR at a 50 ms ISI but not 80 or 100 ms ISI (Baseline, 1.120 ± 0.057; Oxt, 1.721 ± 0.116; p<0.01, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 8 neurons from six mice) (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that oxytocin decreases the probability of glutamate release.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A–B

claim: Oxytocin decreases the probability of glutamate release.
source: Oxytocin application significantly increased PPR at a 50 ms ISI but not 80 or 100 ms ISI (Baseline, 1.120 ± 0.057; Oxt, 1.721 ± 0.116; p<0.01, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 8 neurons from six mice) (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that oxytocin decreases the probability of glutamate release.
evidence: Inferred from the increase in paired-pulse ratio

claim: Blocking either OxtR or the PLC pathway abolished the effect of oxytocin on PPR.
source: Blocking either OxtR or the PLC pathway abolished the effect on PPR. However, in the presence of V1aR antagonist, oxytocin application still significantly increased PPR (Baseline, 0.948 ± 0.076; Oxt, 1.326 ± 0.149; p<0.01, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 8 neurons from five mice) (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–B

claim: In the presence of V1aR antagonist, oxytocin application still significantly increased PPR (Baseline, 0.948 ± 0.076; Oxt, 1.326 ± 0.149; p<0.01, n = 8 neurons from five mice).
source: Blocking either OxtR or the PLC pathway abolished the effect on PPR. However, in the presence of V1aR antagonist, oxytocin application still significantly increased PPR (Baseline, 0.948 ± 0.076; Oxt, 1.326 ± 0.149; p<0.01, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 8 neurons from five mice) (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A–B

claim: Optical activation of oxytocin-positive axons in VTA was sufficient to increase PPR 30 s after light stimulation (Control: Baseline, 1.220 ± 0.127; Light, 1.634 ± 0.195; p<0.01, n = 9 neurons from six mice).
source: Optical activation of oxytocin-positive axons in VTA was sufficient to increase PPR 30 s after light stimulation, consistent with the effect of light stimulation on EPSC amplitude changes (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). These light-evoked changes in PPR, as for the amplitude attenuation, were likewise blocked by the OxtR antagonist (Control: Baseline, 1.220 ± 0.127; Light, 1.634 ± 0.195; p<0.01, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 9 neurons from six mice; L368,899: Baseline, 1.454 ± 0.232; Light, 1.147 ± 0.113; p=0.156, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 6 neurons from four mice) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C, 2D

claim: Light-evoked changes in PPR were blocked by the OxtR antagonist (L368,899: Baseline, 1.454 ± 0.232; Light, 1.147 ± 0.113; p=0.156, n = 6 neurons from four mice).
source: Optical activation of oxytocin-positive axons in VTA was sufficient to increase PPR 30 s after light stimulation, consistent with the effect of light stimulation on EPSC amplitude changes (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). These light-evoked changes in PPR, as for the amplitude attenuation, were likewise blocked by the OxtR antagonist (Control: Baseline, 1.220 ± 0.127; Light, 1.634 ± 0.195; p<0.01, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 9 neurons from six mice; L368,899: Baseline, 1.454 ± 0.232; Light, 1.147 ± 0.113; p=0.156, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 6 neurons from four mice) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: Bath application of oxytocin decreased sEPSC frequency (Baseline, 2.328 ± 0.308 Hz; Oxt, 1.679 ± 0.237 Hz; p<0.05, n = 6 neurons from five mice).
source: Bath application of oxytocin decreased sEPSC frequency (Baseline, 2.328 ± 0.308 Hz; Oxt, 1.679 ± 0.237 Hz; p<0.05, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 6 neurons from five mice), but had no significant effect on sEPSC amplitude (Baseline, 7.741 ± 1.060 pA; Oxt, 8.830 ± 1.389 pA; p=0.094, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test) (Figure 2E–F, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E–F

claim: Bath application of oxytocin had no significant effect on sEPSC amplitude (Baseline, 7.741 ± 1.060 pA; Oxt, 8.830 ± 1.389 pA; p=0.094).
source: Bath application of oxytocin decreased sEPSC frequency (Baseline, 2.328 ± 0.308 Hz; Oxt, 1.679 ± 0.237 Hz; p<0.05, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 6 neurons from five mice), but had no significant effect on sEPSC amplitude (Baseline, 7.741 ± 1.060 pA; Oxt, 8.830 ± 1.389 pA; p=0.094, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test) (Figure 2E–F, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E–F

claim: Oxytocin reduces the probability of glutamate release in excitatory inputs to VTA DA neurons.
source: Together, these results are consistent with the interpretation that oxytocin reduces the probability of glutamate release in excitatory inputs to VTA DA neurons.
evidence: Inferred from PPR and sEPSC frequency data

claim: The amplitude of uEPSCs evoked by the first light pulse recorded in the baseline condition was similar to that recorded in the presence of 1 μM oxytocin.
source: The amplitude of uEPSCs evoked by the first light pulse recorded in the baseline condition was similar to that recorded in the presence of 1 μM oxytocin (Figure 2H–I, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H–I

claim: Oxytocin did not alter the PPR of uEPSCs.
source: Moreover, oxytocin did not alter the PPR of uEPSCs, evaluated using both paired measurements on single spines following oxytocin flow-in (five dendritic spines from four neurons in three mice) or in group data (17 dendritic spines for each condition from 16 neurons in four mice) (Figure 2H and J, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and J

claim: Oxytocin does not modulate glutamatergic receptor properties of VTA DA neurons.
source: These results suggest that oxytocin does not modulate glutamatergic receptor properties of VTA DA neurons, confirming its selective presynaptic effects on synaptic transmission.
evidence: Inferred from glutamate uncaging experiments

claim: Increasing the activity of VTA DA neurons triggers these neurons to release endocannabinoids, which can activate presynaptic cannabinoid CB1 receptors to regulate neurotransmitter release.
source: Previous studies demonstrate that increasing the activity of VTA DA neurons triggers these neurons to release endocannabinoids, which can activate presynaptic cannabinoid CB1 receptors to regulate neurotransmitter release (Melis et al., 2004; Oleson and Cheer, 2012; Riegel and Lupica, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Melis et al., 2004; Oleson and Cheer, 2012; Riegel and Lupica, 2004

claim: The activation of CB receptors with a selective agonist (WIN55212-2) decreases evoked EPSC amplitude (79.77 ± 1.75% of baseline, n = 7 neurons from five mice, p<0.01).
source: We also observed that the activation of CB receptors with a selective agonist (WIN55212-2) decreases evoked EPSC amplitude (79.77 ± 1.75% of baseline, n = 7 neurons from five mice, p<0.01, Wilcoxon signed rank test) and increases PPR (Baseline, 0.780 ± 0.047; WIN, 0.947 ± 0.061; n = 7 neurons from five mice, p<0.01, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test) (Figure 3A,G, Figure 3—source data 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A,G

claim: The activation of CB receptors with WIN55212-2 increases PPR (Baseline, 0.780 ± 0.047; WIN, 0.947 ± 0.061; n = 7 neurons from five mice, p<0.01).
source: We also observed that the activation of CB receptors with a selective agonist (WIN55212-2) decreases evoked EPSC amplitude (79.77 ± 1.75% of baseline, n = 7 neurons from five mice, p<0.01, Wilcoxon signed rank test) and increases PPR (Baseline, 0.780 ± 0.047; WIN, 0.947 ± 0.061; n = 7 neurons from five mice, p<0.01, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test) (Figure 3A,G, Figure 3—source data 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A,G

claim: In the presence of WIN55212-2, oxytocin application failed to modulate the amplitude and PPR of evoked EPSCs in VTA DA neurons.
source: In the presence of WIN55212-2, occluded by CB1 receptor activation, oxytocin application failed to modulate the amplitude and PPR of evoked EPSCs in VTA DA neurons (Figure 3B,G, Figure 3—source data 1, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,G

claim: Blocking cannabinoid CB1 receptors with AM251 abolished oxytocinergic modulation of EPSC amplitude (97.12 ± 2.97% of baseline, p=0.438, n = 6 neurons from three mice).
source: Conversely, blocking cannabinoid CB1 receptors with a selective, high affinity CB1 receptor inverse agonist (AM251) or antagonist (CP945598) abolished oxytocinergic modulation of EPSC amplitude (AM251: 97.12 ± 2.97% of baseline, p=0.438, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 6 neurons from three mice; CP945598: 98.76 ± 2.70% of baseline, p=0.688, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 6 neurons from four mice) and of the PPR of evoked EPSCs (Figure 3C, Figure 3G, Figure 3—source data 1, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C, 3G

claim: Blocking cannabinoid CB1 receptors with CP945598 abolished oxytocinergic modulation of EPSC amplitude (98.76 ± 2.70% of baseline, p=0.688, n = 6 neurons from four mice).
source: Conversely, blocking cannabinoid CB1 receptors with a selective, high affinity CB1 receptor inverse agonist (AM251) or antagonist (CP945598) abolished oxytocinergic modulation of EPSC amplitude (AM251: 97.12 ± 2.97% of baseline, p=0.438, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 6 neurons from three mice; CP945598: 98.76 ± 2.70% of baseline, p=0.688, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 6 neurons from four mice) and of the PPR of evoked EPSCs (Figure 3C, Figure 3G, Figure 3—source data 1, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C, 3G

claim: 2-AG is a primary endocannabinoid synthesized and released by VTA DA neurons.
source: The two major mammalian endocannabinoids are the bioactive lipid 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) and anandamide, and previous evidence suggests that 2-AG is a primary endocannabinoid synthesized and released by VTA DA neurons (Gantz and Bean, 2017; Mátyás et al., 2008; Merrill et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gantz and Bean, 2017; Mátyás et al., 2008; Merrill et al., 2015

claim: PLC cleaves phosphatidylinositol 1,4,5-bisphosphate into diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate; DAG is subsequently converted into 2-AG by DAG lipase.
source: PLC cleaves phosphatidylinositol 1,4,5-bisphosphate into diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate; DAG is subsequently converted into 2-AG by DAG lipase (Di Marzo et al., 1998; Piomelli, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Marzo et al., 1998; Piomelli, 2003

claim: Blocking 2-AG synthesis with THL abolished oxytocinergic effects on the amplitude of evoked EPSCs (99.40 ± 5.54% of baseline, p=0.938, n = 6 neurons from four mice).
source: Brain slices were treated with 1 μM THL for ~1 hr before and during whole-cell recording. Blocking 2-AG synthesis with THL abolished oxytocinergic effects on the amplitude of evoked EPSCs (99.40 ± 5.54% of baseline, p=0.938, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 6 neurons from four mice) (Figure 3D,G, Figure 3—source data 1) and on the PPR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D,G

claim: Intracellular blockade of either the PLC pathway or 2-AG synthesis was sufficient to abolish oxytocinergic effects on the amplitude of evoked EPSCs and PPR.
source: Since bath application of orlistat cannot distinguish cell-autonomous from circuit-level effects of inhibiting 2-AG synthesis, we next carried out experiments using intracellular inhibitors of PLC or 2-AG synthesis (U73122 or THL) in internal recording solution. Intracellular blockade of either the PLC pathway or 2-AG synthesis was sufficient to abolish oxytocinergic effects on the amplitude of evoked EPSCs and PPR (Figure 3E–G, Figure 3—source data 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E–G

claim: In the VTA, oxytocin activates the PLC/DAG lipase pathway to increase 2-AG release, weakening glutamatergic synaptic transmission in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: Therefore, in the VTA, oxytocin activates the PLC/DAG lipase pathway to increase 2-AG release, weakening glutamatergic synaptic transmission in a cell-autonomous manner (Figure 3H).
evidence: Inferred from experimental results with PLC and 2-AG synthesis inhibitors, shown in Figure 3H

claim: Synaptic plasticity of glutamatergic transmission in VTA DA neurons provides a critical substrate relevant to learning and addiction.
source: Synaptic plasticity of glutamatergic transmission in VTA DA neurons provides a critical substrate relevant to learning and addiction (Chen et al., 2010; Kauer and Malenka, 2007; Niehaus et al., 2009), and endocannabinoids play a pivotal role in synaptic plasticity by depressing synaptic transmission on short- and long-term scales (Gerdeman et al., 2002; Di Marzo et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2010; Kauer and Malenka, 2007; Niehaus et al., 2009

claim: Endocannabinoids play a pivotal role in synaptic plasticity by depressing synaptic transmission on short- and long-term scales.
source: Synaptic plasticity of glutamatergic transmission in VTA DA neurons provides a critical substrate relevant to learning and addiction (Chen et al., 2010; Kauer and Malenka, 2007; Niehaus et al., 2009), and endocannabinoids play a pivotal role in synaptic plasticity by depressing synaptic transmission on short- and long-term scales (Gerdeman et al., 2002; Di Marzo et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gerdeman et al., 2002; Di Marzo et al., 1998

claim: Oxytocin perfusion significantly increased the ratio between the amplitudes of the last and first EPSCs in a stimuli train (Control: 0.655 ± 0.131; Oxt: 0.974 ± 0.228; p<0.05, n = 8 neurons from five mice).
source: Oxytocin perfusion significantly increased the ratio between the amplitudes of the last and first EPSCs in a stimuli train (Control: 0.655 ± 0.131; Oxt: 0.974 ± 0.228; p<0.05, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, n = 8 neurons from five mice) (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: In the control condition, EPSC amplitude decreased to 64.22 ± 4.70% of baseline following 10 Hz stimulation (seven neurons from five mice).
source: In the control condition, EPSC amplitude decreased to 64.22 ± 4.70% of baseline following 10 Hz stimulation (seven neurons from five mice) (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—source data 1) and to 64.00 ± 8.19% of baseline following 100 Hz stimulation (five neurons from five mice) (Figure 4F–G, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D–E

claim: In the control condition, EPSC amplitude decreased to 64.00 ± 8.19% of baseline following 100 Hz stimulation (five neurons from five mice).
source: In the control condition, EPSC amplitude decreased to 64.22 ± 4.70% of baseline following 10 Hz stimulation (seven neurons from five mice) (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—source data 1) and to 64.00 ± 8.19% of baseline following 100 Hz stimulation (five neurons from five mice) (Figure 4F–G, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F–G

claim: In the presence of oxytocin, LTD magnitude induced by 10 Hz stimulation was substantially increased (39.42 ± 6.19% of baseline, eight neurons from six mice, p<0.05 vs. control).
source: In the presence of oxytocin, LTD magnitude induced by either stimulation protocol was substantially increased (10 Hz: 39.42 ± 6.19% of baseline, eight neurons from six mice, p<0.05, Mann-Whitney test vs. control; 100 Hz: 34.77 ± 4.18% of baseline, six neurons from six mice, p<0.05, Mann-Whitney test vs. control) (Figure 4D–H, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D–H

claim: In the presence of oxytocin, LTD magnitude induced by 100 Hz stimulation was substantially increased (34.77 ± 4.18% of baseline, six neurons from six mice, p<0.05 vs. control).
source: In the presence of oxytocin, LTD magnitude induced by either stimulation protocol was substantially increased (10 Hz: 39.42 ± 6.19% of baseline, eight neurons from six mice, p<0.05, Mann-Whitney test vs. control; 100 Hz: 34.77 ± 4.18% of baseline, six neurons from six mice, p<0.05, Mann-Whitney test vs. control) (Figure 4D–H, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D–H

claim: Input resistance of VTA DA neurons was similar before and after LTD induction and was not altered by oxytocin.
source: Input resistance of VTA DA neurons was similar before and after LTD induction and was not altered by oxytocin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C

claim: The PPR of EPSCs remained unchanged through LTD induction in the control condition.
source: The PPR of EPSCs remained unchanged through LTD induction in the control condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D), but increased following LTD induction in the presence of oxytocin for both stimulation protocols (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D

claim: PPR increased following LTD induction in the presence of oxytocin for both stimulation protocols.
source: The PPR of EPSCs remained unchanged through LTD induction in the control condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D), but increased following LTD induction in the presence of oxytocin for both stimulation protocols (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D

claim: In the presence of oxytocin and OxtR antagonist L368,899, LTD magnitude induced by 100 Hz stimulation was similar to that in the control condition (63.46 ± 8.48% of baseline, six neurons from four mice).
source: In the presence of oxytocin and either OxtR antagonist L368,899 or the CB1 receptor inverse agonist AM251, LTD magnitude induced by 100 Hz stimulation was similar to that in the control condition and smaller than the LTD magnitude in the presence of oxytocin (L368,899: 63.46 ± 8.48% of baseline, six neurons from four mice; AM251: 55.77 ± 4.69% of baseline, seven neurons from four mice, p<0.05, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's Multiple Comparison post hoc test) (Figure 4F–H, Figure 4—source data 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F–H

claim: In the presence of oxytocin and CB1 receptor inverse agonist AM251, LTD magnitude induced by 100 Hz stimulation was similar to that in the control condition (55.77 ± 4.69% of baseline, seven neurons from four mice).
source: In the presence of oxytocin and either OxtR antagonist L368,899 or the CB1 receptor inverse agonist AM251, LTD magnitude induced by 100 Hz stimulation was similar to that in the control condition and smaller than the LTD magnitude in the presence of oxytocin (L368,899: 63.46 ± 8.48% of baseline, six neurons from four mice; AM251: 55.77 ± 4.69% of baseline, seven neurons from four mice, p<0.05, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's Multiple Comparison post hoc test) (Figure 4F–H, Figure 4—source data 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F–H

claim: Oxytocin modulates both short- and long-term synaptic plasticity in VTA DA neurons by presynaptic mechanisms mediated by endocannabinoids.
source: Together, oxytocin modulates both short- and long-term synaptic plasticity in VTA DA neurons by presynaptic mechanisms mediated by endocannabinoids.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results on short-term and long-term plasticity

claim: Brain regions that send glutamatergic projections to the VTA – but not the VTA DA neurons themselves – are known to express the CB1 receptors.
source: While brain regions that send glutamatergic projections to the VTA – but not the VTA DA neurons themselves – are known to express the CB1 receptors (Mátyás et al., 2008), it remains unknown whether specific groups of VTA-projecting neurons selectively express this receptor.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mátyás et al., 2008

claim: Few Th+ neurons in the VTA co-localized with Cnr1+ puncta (<7%, n = 1258 Th+ neurons from three mice).
source: DA neurons were identified by labeling for tyrosine hydroxylase (Th), and few Th+ neurons in the VTA co-localized with Cnr1+ puncta (<7%, n = 1258 Th+ neurons from three mice) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: In the mPFC, the vast majority of glutamatergic neurons projecting to VTA (GRB+/Slc17a7+) co-localized with strong Cnr1 signal (143 GRB+/Slc17a7+/Cnr1+ neurons of 188 GRB+/Slc17a7+ neurons from three mice).
source: In the mPFC, Slc17a7 probe was used to label glutamatergic neurons; there, the vast majority of glutamatergic neurons projecting to VTA (GRB+/Slc17a7+) co-localized with strong Cnr1 signal (143 GRB+/Slc17a7+/Cnr1+neurons of 188 GRB+/Slc17a7+ neurons from three mice) (Figure 5D–E, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D–E

claim: LHb had almost no Cnr1 expression, so triple-labeled neurons were rare (4 GRB+/Slc17a6+/Cnr1+ neurons of 178 GRB+/Slc17a6+ neurons from two mice).
source: However, LHb had almost no Cnr1 expression, so triple-labeled neurons were rare (4 GRB+/Slc17a6+/Cnr1+neurons of 178 GRB+/Slc17a6+ neurons from two mice) (Figure 5D–E, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Over 70% of GRB+/Slc17a6+ neurons in the PPN co-localized with Cnr1 signal (306 GRB+/Slc17a6+/Cnr1+ neurons of 401 GRB+/Slc17a6+ neurons from three mice).
source: In contrast, over 70% of GRB+/Slc17a6+ neurons in the PPN co-localized with Cnr1 signal (306 GRB+/Slc17a6+/Cnr1+neurons of 401 GRB+/Slc17a6+ neurons from three mice) (Figure 5D–E, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D–E

claim: Following mPFC targeting, 9/30 VTA DA neurons from four mice responded to light stimulation, and oxytocin application attenuated the amplitude of light-evoked EPSCs (73.35 ± 3.83% of baseline, p<0.05, n = 6 neurons from four mice).
source: Following mPFC targeting, 9/30 VTA DA neurons from four mice responded to light stimulation, and oxytocin application attenuated the amplitude of light-evoked EPSCs (73.35 ± 3.83% of baseline, p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 6 neurons from four mice) (Figure 6B–C, Figure 6—source data 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B–C

claim: After PPN transduction, 8/10 VTA neurons from two mice responded to light stimulation, and oxytocin significantly dampened light-evoked EPSCs (82.55 ± 0.76% of baseline, p<0.05, n = 7 neurons from two mice).
source: After PPN transduction, 8/10 VTA neurons from two mice responded to light stimulation, and oxytocin also significantly dampened light-evoked EPSCs (82.55 ± 0.76% of baseline, p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 7 neurons from two mice) (Figure 6B–C, Figure 6—source data 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B–C

claim: With ChR2 virus targeted to the LHb, while 8/21 VTA DA neurons responded to light stimulation, oxytocin had no effect on the amplitude of evoked EPSCs (94.84 ± 2.27% of baseline, p=0.219, n = 7 neurons from four mice).
source: In contrast, with ChR2 virus targeted to the LHb, while 8/21 VTA DA neurons responded to light stimulation, oxytocin had no effect on the amplitude of evoked EPSCs (94.84 ± 2.27% of baseline, p=0.219, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 7 neurons from four mice) (Figure 6B–C, Figure 6—source data 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B–C

claim: Distinct sources of glutamate converging on individual VTA DA neurons are differentially regulated by oxytocin based on CB1 receptor expression.
source: These data likely indicate that distinct sources of glutamate converging on individual VTA DA neurons are differentially regulated by oxytocin based on CB1 receptor expression, but an alternative interpretation of these results is that VTA DA neurons receiving inputs from lateral habenula selectively lack OxtRs.
evidence: Inferred from pathway-specific optogenetic stimulation experiments

claim: Oxytocin inhibits excitatory synaptic transmission via OxtR and retrograde endocannabinoid signaling.
source: Here, we find that oxytocin inhibits excitatory synaptic transmission via OxtR and retrograde endocannabinoid signaling, modulating both short- and long-term plasticity in a subset of VTA DA neurons through presynaptic mechanisms.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: VTA-targeting glutamatergic neurons from the mPFC and the PPN, but not the LHb, express the CB1 receptor.
source: Specifically, VTA-targeting glutamatergic neurons from the mPFC and the PPN, but not the LHb, express the CB1 receptor.
evidence: Supported by FISH data

claim: Oxytocin gates information flow into reward circuits in a temporally selective and pathway-specific manner.
source: Thus, oxytocin gates information flow into reward circuits in a temporally selective and pathway-specific manner.
evidence: Summary conclusion from experimental findings

source: For example, the lateral habenula acts as a source of negative reward signals for DA neurons (Lammel et al., 2012; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007).

source: Meanwhile, mPFC glutamatergic afferents increase VTA activity and may promote the development of addiction (Gariano and Groves, 1988; Wu et al., 2013), and pedunculopontine glutamatergic afferents to VTA DA neurons drive motivated behavior (Yoo et al., 2017).

source: This study also reported a direct facilitation of tonic activity in VTA DA neurons, in response to oxytocin receptor agonist application, consistent with our prior observations (Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hung et al., 2017 and Xiao et al., 2017

claim: Medial NAc-projecting VTA DA neurons are innervated by glutamatergic axons from lateral hypothalamus, lateral habenula and dorsal raphe nuclei.
source: This difference in selection is important because DA neurons projecting to distinct regions of NAc receive different glutamatergic inputs (Beier et al., 2015). Medial NAc-projecting VTA DA neurons are innervated by glutamatergic axons from lateral hypothalamus, lateral habenula and dorsal raphe nuclei (Beier et al., 2015), where we do not observe extensive presence of CB1Rs in glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to Beier et al., 2015

claim: Spermine can modulate and inhibit the PLC cascade.

evidence: Supported by citations to Sechi et al., 1978; Wojcikiewicz and Fain, 1988

claim: In the striatum, cortical glutamatergic inputs, but not thalamostriatal ones, display CB1 receptor-dependent LTD.

claim: Oxytocin has neuroprotective properties.
